title: DualHeads: Reward-tilted few-step diffusion made simple

paper.title: DualHeads: Reward-tilted few-step diffusion made simple
paper.abstract: Abstract Distilled diffusion models generate high-quality images in a few sampling steps, but aligning them with task requirements and human preferences is difficult. Methods developed for multi-step diffusion models rely on differentiable rewards, or on score fields and stochastic trajectories that distilled generators may lack. We ask whether a few-step generator can be adapted using only external reward evaluations and reference samples, and show that two binary classifiers suffice. Our method, DualHeads, implements them as lightweight heads on a frozen diffusion backbone. The reward head learns which samples of the same prompt score higher, the reference head separates reference images from generated ones, and the generator maximizes a weighted sum of their logits. When the heads are optimal, this objective is KL-regularized maximization of the learned reward, and the ratio of head weights sets the regularization strength. Empirically, with both rule-based and model-based rewards, a few-step DualHeads generator reaches task rewards close to those of 40-step reinforcement learning methods while preserving image quality, at no extra inference cost. We hope that this simple and elegant dual-head formulation will help advance few-step reward-tilted generation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion distillation ( Song et al., 2023 ; Yin et al., 2024b ; Sauer et al., 2024a ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) turns powerful diffusion models ( Song et al., 2021 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) into few-step generators that produce high-quality samples in a handful of network evaluations, bringing applications such as real-time interactive video generation within reach ( Yin et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) . Speed alone, however, does not make a sample correct: a distilled student inherits the teacher’s failures, and may still misspell the prompted text, miscount objects, or ignore the requested style. Such failures are readily caught by external evaluators, such as text recognizers, object detectors, or preference models. Using these external evaluators as rewards to post-train a generator is now standard practice for diffusion models ( Lee et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2024 ) . Existing methods fall into two families, each typically addressing only one side of this setting. First, reinforcement learning (RL) with black-box rewards has succeeded for multi-step diffusion models, through policy gradients that reinforce high-reward denoising steps ( Black et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Xue et al., 2025 ) or forward-process objectives ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Xue et al., 2026 ; Choi et al., 2026a ; Lee et al., 2026 ) . These, however, rely on what distillation removes: policy gradients estimate updates from stochastic multi-step rollouts, which become high-variance with only a few steps, and forward-process objectives need a score or velocity field that a distilled generator need not preserve. Second, methods designed for few-step generators pay for the step constraint elsewhere: they backpropagate through a differentiable reward ( Luo, 2025 ) which may not always be feasible, match the generator to the original multi-step model (the teacher) using its score and a second diffusion model fitted to the generator’s samples ( Luo et al., 2026a ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026a , e.g.,) , or adapt multi-step RL specifically to flow-map generators such as consistency models and MeanFlow ( Li et al., 2026c ; Huang et al., 2026b ) . Methods from both families rely on something beyond samples and black-box scores: trajectory likelihoods, a score field, reward gradients, or the teacher’s score. In practice, however, the only thing any few-step generator is guaranteed to provide is samples. This leads to our central question: given only its own samples, black-box reward evaluations, and examples of high-quality images from a reference model, can we tilt a few-step generator toward higher reward regions while keeping it close to those images? We show that this can be done with only one backbone network and two binary classifiers. We begin with the standard reference-regularized RL objective ( Levine, 2018 ) , which maximizes the expected reward while penalizing the reverse KL divergence to the reference distribution to prevent reward hacking. Its optimum is the reference distribution reweighted by the exponentiated reward. The two terms are, however, hard to optimize directly in our setting, since we treat the reward as a black box and the KL term depends on the density ratio between the generator and the reference. Our key observation is that both can be replaced by quantities learned through classification. This leads to DualHeads, a simple framework consisting of two identical lightweight heads on a shared frozen diffusion backbone. A reward head learns which samples are better from their black-box rewards: for multiple generations of the same prompt, rewards are normalized within the group and converted into soft optimality labels. A reference head distinguishes noised reference images from noised generator predictions. Both heads are trained with the same binary cross-entropy objective and updated online as the generator updates. To update the generator, we evaluate the two heads on a noised generator prediction and maximize a weighted sum of their logits. Gradients pass through both heads and a single generator forward pass; the sampled trajectory and the head parameters remain fixed. The heads are discarded at inference. We note that at the optimum of the reference head, maximizing this weighted sum is equivalent to the reference-regularized objective from above, with the reward-head logit in place of the reward and the ratio of head weights setting the regularization strength. We evaluate DualHeads at a four-step setup on complementary modern reward functions, including visual text rendering (OCR), compositional generation (GenEval), and human preference (HPS, PickScore, etc.). Compared with existing methods, DualHeads achieves on-par performance in the few-step regime while preserving generation quality. It raises OCR accuracy from 0.59 0.59 to 0.92 0.92 and GenEval from 0.63 0.63 to 0.90 0.90 over the base model, and gives the best HPSv3 on Z-Image ( Fig. 1 ). Our contributions are: • We introduce DualHeads, a simple framework that adapts few-step generators from reward evaluations and reference samples alone, using two classifier heads on a frozen backbone. • We show that, with optimal heads, the weighted-logit generator objective is a reverse-KL-regularized reward objective whose temperature is set by the head-weight ratio. • We provide empirical results with both rule-based and model-based rewards, showing that a four-step student reaches task rewards close to 40-step RL methods while preserving quality.

sections.heading: Step distillation of diffusion models.
sections.text: Progressive and consistency distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ) turn a pretrained diffusion model into a few-step generator that covers the sampling trajectory in a small number of large jumps. Latent consistency models ( Luo et al., 2023 ) extend this to text-to-image latent diffusion. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) ( Yin et al., 2024b ) instead matches the student’s output distribution to the teacher’s by following the gradient from a score difference, which requires an auxiliary network that tracks the student’s score online. DMD2 ( Yin et al., 2024a ) stabilizes this estimator and adds an adversarial term on real data, and TDM ( Luo et al., 2025 ) extends the matching to every step of the sampling trajectory. Parallel work relies on adversarial supervision. ADD ( Sauer et al., 2024b ) distills with a discriminator on pretrained image features, and LADD ( Sauer et al., 2024a ) moves the discriminator onto frozen features of the teacher diffusion model itself. DualHeads is built on top of a few-step distilled diffusion model. Our reference head follows LADD’s design of heads on frozen diffusion features.

sections.heading: Reward optimization of diffusion models.
sections.text: Methods for optimizing a reward differ mainly in how the reward signal reaches the generator. Differentiable rewards can be backpropagated through directly ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Clark et al., 2024 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ) , but black-box rewards cannot. Reinforcement learning (RL) removes this requirement: DDPO ( Black et al., 2024 ) and DPOK ( Fan et al., 2023 ) use policy gradients, and Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) and DanceGRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) adapt group-relative policy optimization ( Shao et al., 2024 ) to flow models. These methods need transition likelihoods along stochastic multi-step rollouts, which recent work avoids by training on the forward process. DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) contrasts positive and negative samples under clipped group-relative optimality labels, CRD ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) matches prompt-centered rewards to cancel an intractable normalizer, and AWM ( Xue et al., 2026 ) , RAM ( Bergmeister et al., 2026 ) , RVM ( Choi et al., 2026a ) , and DGPO ( Luo et al., 2026b ) use related advantage- or reward-weighted targets. In all of them, the reward serves only as a sample weight or a regression target, and no explicit reward model is learned. DualHeads uses labels of the same form as DiffusionNFT, but fits them with an explicit classifier and guides the student through that classifier’s input gradient.

sections.heading: Reward optimization coupled with distillation.
sections.text: Other methods optimize the reward inside a distillation pipeline and differ mainly in what keeps the generator close to good images while the reward is optimized. Most rely on a teacher. Some combine a reward objective with distribution matching ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026 ) ; for example, RTDMD ( Huang et al., 2026a ) minimizes a KL divergence to a reward-tilted teacher. Closest to our setting, TDM-R1 ( Luo et al., 2026a ) post-trains a few-step student with non-differentiable rewards by learning a diffusion-model surrogate reward, and regularizes it with trajectory distribution matching, which requires the teacher and an online fake score. Flow-OPD ( Fang et al., 2026 ) and DiffusionOPD ( Li et al., 2026a ) first train task-specific teachers with RL and then distill them into one student, without reducing the step count. REST ( Li et al., 2026b ) co-trains an eight-step student with an evolving teacher. Others do without a teacher. MeanFlowNFT ( Huang et al., 2026b ) applies forward-process RL to a distilled four-step generator, anchored to a frozen EMA of itself, and Self-OPD ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) scores branched student rollouts against the student’s own deterministic trajectory. Reward Lightning ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) is closest in architecture: it jointly distills a video teacher into a few-step generator with discriminator and reward heads on one frozen backbone, but its reward head is pretrained on preference pairs and kept frozen. sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: DualHeads adapts a few-step generator so that its samples score higher under an external reward while staying close to a reference distribution. For this, we use two binary classifiers on a shared frozen backbone: one learns reference fidelity , the other reward optimality . Section 3.1 describes the few-step generation setting and the corresponding reward-tilted target. Section 3.2 defines the two classifier objectives and Section 3.3 gives the single utility the generator maximizes.

sections.heading: Training and inference.
sections.text: Training alternates between classifier and generator updates at each iteration ( Algorithm 1 ). For each prompt in the batch, we sample K K few-step rollouts and evaluate their black-box rewards. The resulting rewards are used to calculate the soft label and then supervise the reward head. sections.heading: Models and rewards.
sections.text: We use SD3.5 Medium (SD3.5-M) and Z-Image as base models, trained at a resolution of 512 2 512^{2} . With SD3.5-M, we study two non-differentiable rewards, OCR and GenEval, trained separately, and one multi-reward setting, PickScore + CLIPScore + HPSv2.1. For Z-Image, we use HPSv3 as reward. The generators are initialized as few-step distilled diffusion models. Prompt dataset. For OCR and GenEval, we use the corresponding training and test sets from Flow-GRPO. For all other rewards, we train on Pick-a-Pic ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) and evaluate on DrawBench ( Saharia et al., 2022 ) . Regardless of the training reward, we additionally evaluate every trained model on the OCR and GenEval test sets using their respective rewards. Reference pools. For OCR and GenEval, we generate reference pools with the base model using training-set prompts and 20 steps of sampling. For OCR, we generate eight candidates for each of 5,000 prompts and retain the highest-scoring candidate for each prompt only if its OCR reward is at least 0.6 0.6 . For GenEval, we construct a separate pool using 10,000 rows sampled from the GenEval training set. For all other rewards, we use the existing Pick-a-Pic images as the reference pool. Alternatively, an external model can generate the reference pool from the same training prompts: we use Nano Banana, Google’s proprietary image-generation model ( Google DeepMind, 2026 ) . Training and evaluation. Following prior work, we fine-tune the student generator using LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) with rank 32 32 and α = 64 \alpha=64 . Each epoch consists of 48 prompt groups, with group size K = 24 K{=}24 for the main results and K = 8 K{=}8 for all ablations. By default, the reward head is warmed up on samples from the reference distribution with scores from the reward, so that the generator does not receive noisy gradients early in training. This warm-up uses 1000 steps, a very small training budget compared with a full run ( Section 4.3 ). Both training and evaluation use four sampling steps, unless stated otherwise, with the LCM sampler ( Luo et al., 2023 ) and no classifier-free guidance (CFG scale 1 1 ). We also evaluate the trained models using Aesthetic and ImageReward on the same evaluation set. Details in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Text rendering.
sections.text: With four steps, DualHeads raises OCR accuracy from 0.59 0.59 to 0.92 0.92 ( 0.91 0.91 with two), on par with Flow-GRPO with KL and CRD ( Table 1 ). AWM without CFG and DiffusionNFT reach 0.97 0.97 but lose image quality (negative ImageReward; HPS ≈ 0.20 \approx 0.20 vs. 0.279 0.279 for the base model). DualHeads instead improves all quality and preference scores over the base model, with the highest ImageReward ( 1.10 1.10 ) and HPS ( 0.300 0.300 , tied with REST) among OCR-trained models. Among few-step methods, only TDM-R1 ( 0.95 0.95 ) and REST ( 0.96 0.96 ) score higher, using the teacher’s score and 8 NFE with an extra PickScore reward, respectively. sections.heading: Qualitative comparison.
sections.text: In Fig. 3 , DualHeads renders all five OCR texts correctly and blends them into the scene (neon signs, a trail sign, a mural, an envelope). MeanFlowNFT prints the text on flat black plates and misspells “Upgrades Available”, RTDMD mirrors or misspells words (“Propety”, “Readiing”), and TDM-R1 adds a word (“Clup”). On GenEval, the baselines draw isolated objects on plain backgrounds (RSM also misses the TV), while DualHeads often places them in context, e.g., a ski in snow or a zebra beside a bed. The Nano Banana pool makes samples more photographic; it keeps OCR at 0.92 0.92 but lowers GenEval to 0.73 0.73 ( Section 4.3 ).

sections.heading: Warming up the reward head buys speed, not quality.
sections.text: At two points of the sweep we initialize the reward head either from the warmed-up head used by default ( Section 4.1 ) or from scratch, holding everything else fixed ( Fig. 4(b) ). A fresh head starts far behind: 0.497 0.497 and 0.459 0.459 below its warmed-up twin at the first checkpoint, as the generator receives noisy scoring signals before the reward head is well-trained. It recovers by step 3000 3000 , some 8 8 of the ≈ 20 \approx\!20 wall-clock hours per run, and converges to within 0.003 0.003 and 0.004 0.004 of the warmed-up runs, far inside the ± 0.029 \pm 0.029 and ± 0.038 \pm 0.038 intervals. As this holds at both weight settings, the reward head warm-up only speeds up training, at a very small cost, and does not change the final result.

sections.heading: Choice of data source for the reference pool.
sections.text: For the same training prompts, we compare a base-model pool , sampled from the base model, with a Nano Banana pool generated through its API. The two differ well beyond their scores: base-model samples keep SD3.5-M’s flat lighting, sparse layouts and misspelled words, whereas Nano Banana images are photographic, correctly lettered and set in fuller scenes. On OCR, the generator adopts the pool’s style without losing the text (last two rows of Fig. 3 ; more samples in Fig. 7 ): OCR stays at 0.92 0.92 ( Table 1 ), the aesthetic score rises from 5.46 5.46 to 5.62 5.62 , ImageReward, PickScore and HPS barely change, and CLIPScore drops from 28.75 28.75 to 26.86 26.86 . GenEval, however, falls from 0.90 0.90 to 0.73 0.73 , showing that the pool can also affect compositional accuracy. The two heads thus largely divide the work: the reward head governs what the reward measures, and the reference head governs everything the reward leaves unspecified, which is set by the reference pool.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented DualHeads, a simple method for adapting few-step diffusion generators using only external reward evaluations and reference samples. It turns KL-regularized reward maximization into two binary classification problems, solved by lightweight heads on a frozen diffusion backbone. With four steps, it reaches OCR and GenEval scores of 0.92 0.92 and 0.90 0.90 , comparable to RL methods with 40–80 NFE, while improving all quality and preference scores over the base model, and gives the best HPSv3 on Z-Image-Turbo. The two heads divide the work: the reward head sets what the reward measures, and the reference pool largely sets the rest, such as style. Appendix A discusses limitations and future directions.

sections.heading: Appendix A Limitations and future work
sections.text: We see three main limitations. Idealized analysis. Our analysis in Section 3.3 assumes optimal heads and a fixed reward head. In practice, the heads are only approximately optimal, and the reward head is refit on samples from the current generator, so the target moves during training. We also have no convergence guarantee for the alternating updates. Learned reward. The generator is trained against the reward head, not the reward itself, so it inherits both the errors of the head and the flaws of the external reward. The reference head keeps samples close to the reference pool, but it cannot tell when the generator is exploiting the reward. Reference pool. Fidelity is measured against the pool, so the generator also picks up properties that the reward ignores, such as style and composition ( Section 4.3 ). Several directions remain open. A convergence analysis of the alternating updates would put the method on firmer ground. The reward head also deserves a wider study, covering its architecture design, its backbone features analysis, the noise levels it sees, and so on. Richer reference pools, with several references per prompt or with real images, are another natural extension. Practically, DualHeads could be applied during distillation, at higher resolutions, and to few-step video generators.

sections.heading: OCR.
sections.text: Text is recognized with PaddleOCR ( Cui et al., 2025 ) . The target string w w is the first double-quoted span of the prompt; prompts without a non-empty target are excluded before scoring. Recognized segments with positive confidence are concatenated, in the order returned by the OCR engine, into a string w ^ \hat{w} . Both strings are lowercased and ASCII spaces are removed; other whitespace, punctuation, and Unicode forms are left unchanged. The reward is r OCR ​ ( w ^ , w ) = { 1 , if w is a substring of w ^ , max ⁡ { 0 , 1 − d Lev ​ ( w ^ , w ) / | w | } , otherwise , r_{\mathrm{OCR}}(\hat{w},w)=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if $w$ is a substring of $\hat{w}$},\\ \max\{0,\,1-d_{\mathrm{Lev}}(\hat{w},w)/|w|\},&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (13) where d Lev d_{\mathrm{Lev}} is the Levenshtein distance and | w | |w| the target length; recognition failures receive zero. The reward therefore tolerates extra text and ignores case and spacing.

sections.heading: GenEval.
sections.text: The generator is trained on the GenEval training prompts from Flow-GRPO, with a reference pool of 10,000 rows sampled from the GenEval training set ( Section 4.1 ). We score images with the GenEval evaluator ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) , as implemented in the Flow-GRPO reward server ( Liu et al., 2025 ) : Mask2Former ( Cheng et al., 2022 ) (Swin-S, trained on COCO) detects objects with confidence above 0.3 0.3 ( 0.9 0.9 for counting), CLIP ViT-L/14 ( Radford et al., 2021 ) classifies their colors, and relative positions are read from box centroids. A requested object with count n n and n ^ \hat{n} detections earns the credit 1 − | n − n ^ | / n 1-|n-\hat{n}|/n and, only if n ^ = n \hat{n}=n , a further credit for its color or position. The dense training reward is the mean of these credits, while the strict score is 1 1 only if every requirement is met exactly. Tables 1 and 5 report the official GenEval accuracy, averaged over its six task categories.

sections.heading: Multi-reward (PickScore + CLIPScore + HPSv2.1).
sections.text: The generator is trained on Pick-a-Pic prompts, with the existing Pick-a-Pic images as the reference pool ( Section 4.1 ). The three scores are PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) (the PickScore_v1 checkpoint, on a CLIP ViT-H/14 backbone), CLIPScore ( Hessel et al., 2021 ) with OpenAI CLIP ViT-L/14 ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , and HPSv2.1 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) (on a CLIP ViT-H/14 backbone). Following DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , the training reward is the sum of the three scores with equal weights, and the labels of Eq. 8 are computed from this sum.

sections.heading: HPSv3 (Z-Image).
sections.text: The generator is initialized from Z-Image-Turbo ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , the few-step distilled version of Z-Image ( Z-Image Team et al., 2025 ) , and fine-tuned with the same LoRA configuration as SD3.5-M ( Section 4.1 ). The reward is HPSv3 ( Ma et al., 2025 ) , with the released checkpoint built on Qwen2-VL. As in the multi-reward setting, we train on Pick-a-Pic prompts with the Pick-a-Pic images as the reference pool, and evaluate on DrawBench prompts. The reward weight is λ R = 25 \lambda_{R}=25 , and Table 2 reports EMA weights after 120 training iterations, sampled with two and four steps; all other settings follow Table 3 .

Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, LJK Vicky Kalogeiton Affiliation: LIX, École Polytechnique, CNRS, IPP Abstract Distilled diffusion models generate high-quality images in a few sampling steps, but aligning them with task requirements and human preferences is difficult. Methods developed for multi-step diffusion models rely on differentiable rewards, or on score fields and stochastic trajectories that distilled generators may lack. We ask whether a few-step generator can be adapted using only external reward evaluations and reference samples, and show that two binary classifiers suffice. Our method, DualHeads, implements them as lightweight heads on a frozen diffusion backbone. The reward head learns which samples of the same prompt score higher, the reference head separates reference images from generated ones, and the generator maximizes a weighted sum of their logits. When the heads are optimal, this objective is KL-regularized maximization of the learned reward, and the ratio of head weights sets the regularization strength. Empirically, with both rule-based and model-based rewards, a few-step DualHeads generator reaches task rewards close to those of 40-step reinforcement learning methods while preserving image quality, at no extra inference cost. We hope that this simple and elegant dual-head formulation will help advance few-step reward-tilted generation. Figure 1: Four-step samples from DualHeads. Z-Image-Turbo ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) fine-tuned with DualHeads using the HPSv3 reward ( Ma et al., 2025 ) . 1 Introduction Diffusion distillation ( Song et al., 2023 ; Yin et al., 2024b ; Sauer et al., 2024a ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) turns powerful diffusion models ( Song et al., 2021 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) into few-step generators that produce high-quality samples in a handful of network evaluations, bringing applications such as real-time interactive video generation within reach ( Yin et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) . Speed alone, however, does not make a sample correct: a distilled student inherits the teacher’s failures, and may still misspell the prompted text, miscount objects, or ignore the requested style. Such failures are readily caught by external evaluators, such as text recognizers, object detectors, or preference models. Using these external evaluators as rewards to post-train a generator is now standard practice for diffusion models ( Lee et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2024 ) . Existing methods fall into two families, each typically addressing only one side of this setting. First, reinforcement learning (RL) with black-box rewards has succeeded for multi-step diffusion models, through policy gradients that reinforce high-reward denoising steps ( Black et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Xue et al., 2025 ) or forward-process objectives ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Xue et al., 2026 ; Choi et al., 2026a ; Lee et al., 2026 ) . These, however, rely on what distillation removes: policy gradients estimate updates from stochastic multi-step rollouts, which become high-variance with only a few steps, and forward-process objectives need a score or velocity field that a distilled generator need not preserve. Second, methods designed for few-step generators pay for the step constraint elsewhere: they backpropagate through a differentiable reward ( Luo, 2025 ) which may not always be feasible, match the generator to the original multi-step model (the teacher) using its score and a second diffusion model fitted to the generator’s samples ( Luo et al., 2026a ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026a , e.g.,) , or adapt multi-step RL specifically to flow-map generators such as consistency models and MeanFlow ( Li et al., 2026c ; Huang et al., 2026b ) . Methods from both families rely on something beyond samples and black-box scores: trajectory likelihoods, a score field, reward gradients, or the teacher’s score. In practice, however, the only thing any few-step generator is guaranteed to provide is samples. This leads to our central question: given only its own samples, black-box reward evaluations, and examples of high-quality images from a reference model, can we tilt a few-step generator toward higher reward regions while keeping it close to those images? We show that this can be done with only one backbone network and two binary classifiers. We begin with the standard reference-regularized RL objective ( Levine, 2018 ) , which maximizes the expected reward while penalizing the reverse KL divergence to the reference distribution to prevent reward hacking. Its optimum is the reference distribution reweighted by the exponentiated reward. The two terms are, however, hard to optimize directly in our setting, since we treat the reward as a black box and the KL term depends on the density ratio between the generator and the reference. Our key observation is that both can be replaced by quantities learned through classification. This leads to DualHeads, a simple framework consisting of two identical lightweight heads on a shared frozen diffusion backbone. A reward head learns which samples are better from their black-box rewards: for multiple generations of the same prompt, rewards are normalized within the group and converted into soft optimality labels. A reference head distinguishes noised reference images from noised generator predictions. Both heads are trained with the same binary cross-entropy objective and updated online as the generator updates. To update the generator, we evaluate the two heads on a noised generator prediction and maximize a weighted sum of their logits. Gradients pass through both heads and a single generator forward pass; the sampled trajectory and the head parameters remain fixed. The heads are discarded at inference. We note that at the optimum of the reference head, maximizing this weighted sum is equivalent to the reference-regularized objective from above, with the reward-head logit in place of the reward and the ratio of head weights setting the regularization strength. We evaluate DualHeads at a four-step setup on complementary modern reward functions, including visual text rendering (OCR), compositional generation (GenEval), and human preference (HPS, PickScore, etc.). Compared with existing methods, DualHeads achieves on-par performance in the few-step regime while preserving generation quality. It raises OCR accuracy from 0.59 0.59 to 0.92 0.92 and GenEval from 0.63 0.63 to 0.90 0.90 over the base model, and gives the best HPSv3 on Z-Image ( Fig. 1 ). Our contributions are: • We introduce DualHeads, a simple framework that adapts few-step generators from reward evaluations and reference samples alone, using two classifier heads on a frozen backbone. • We show that, with optimal heads, the weighted-logit generator objective is a reverse-KL-regularized reward objective whose temperature is set by the head-weight ratio. • We provide empirical results with both rule-based and model-based rewards, showing that a four-step student reaches task rewards close to 40-step RL methods while preserving quality. 2 Related Work Step distillation of diffusion models. Progressive and consistency distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ) turn a pretrained diffusion model into a few-step generator that covers the sampling trajectory in a small number of large jumps. Latent consistency models ( Luo et al., 2023 ) extend this to text-to-image latent diffusion. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) ( Yin et al., 2024b ) instead matches the student’s output distribution to the teacher’s by following the gradient from a score difference, which requires an auxiliary network that tracks the student’s score online. DMD2 ( Yin et al., 2024a ) stabilizes this estimator and adds an adversarial term on real data, and TDM ( Luo et al., 2025 ) extends the matching to every step of the sampling trajectory. Parallel work relies on adversarial supervision. ADD ( Sauer et al., 2024b ) distills with a discriminator on pretrained image features, and LADD ( Sauer et al., 2024a ) moves the discriminator onto frozen features of the teacher diffusion model itself. DualHeads is built on top of a few-step distilled diffusion model. Our reference head follows LADD’s design of heads on frozen diffusion features. Reward optimization of diffusion models. Methods for optimizing a reward differ mainly in how the reward signal reaches the generator. Differentiable rewards can be backpropagated through directly ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Clark et al., 2024 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ) , but black-box rewards cannot. Reinforcement learning (RL) removes this requirement: DDPO ( Black et al., 2024 ) and DPOK ( Fan et al., 2023 ) use policy gradients, and Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) and DanceGRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) adapt group-relative policy optimization ( Shao et al., 2024 ) to flow models. These methods need transition likelihoods along stochastic multi-step rollouts, which recent work avoids by training on the forward process. DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) contrasts positive and negative samples under clipped group-relative optimality labels, CRD ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) matches prompt-centered rewards to cancel an intractable normalizer, and AWM ( Xue et al., 2026 ) , RAM ( Bergmeister et al., 2026 ) , RVM ( Choi et al., 2026a ) , and DGPO ( Luo et al., 2026b ) use related advantage- or reward-weighted targets. In all of them, the reward serves only as a sample weight or a regression target, and no explicit reward model is learned. DualHeads uses labels of the same form as DiffusionNFT, but fits them with an explicit classifier and guides the student through that classifier’s input gradient. Reward optimization coupled with distillation. Other methods optimize the reward inside a distillation pipeline and differ mainly in what keeps the generator close to good images while the reward is optimized. Most rely on a teacher. Some combine a reward objective with distribution matching ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026 ) ; for example, RTDMD ( Huang et al., 2026a ) minimizes a KL divergence to a reward-tilted teacher. Closest to our setting, TDM-R1 ( Luo et al., 2026a ) post-trains a few-step student with non-differentiable rewards by learning a diffusion-model surrogate reward, and regularizes it with trajectory distribution matching, which requires the teacher and an online fake score. Flow-OPD ( Fang et al., 2026 ) and DiffusionOPD ( Li et al., 2026a ) first train task-specific teachers with RL and then distill them into one student, without reducing the step count. REST ( Li et al., 2026b ) co-trains an eight-step student with an evolving teacher. Others do without a teacher. MeanFlowNFT ( Huang et al., 2026b ) applies forward-process RL to a distilled four-step generator, anchored to a frozen EMA of itself, and Self-OPD ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) scores branched student rollouts against the student’s own deterministic trajectory. Reward Lightning ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) is closest in architecture: it jointly distills a video teacher into a few-step generator with discriminator and reward heads on one frozen backbone, but its reward head is pretrained on preference pairs and kept frozen. DualHeads instead post-trains a distilled generator and refits its reward head online, on pointwise group-relative labels from black-box rewards, while its reference head keeps the generator close to the reference pool. ∼ x 0 N ( 0 , I ) N f θ x 1 ϵ ′ x t i f θ ^ x 1 ϵ x t F ( x t , c , t ) D ϕ R ψ = s + ⁢ λ D D ϕ ⁢ λ R R ψ = ⁢ ∇ θ L f ( θ ) - E [ ∇ θ s ] θ Figure 2: Generator update of DualHeads. We use SD3.5 Medium (SD3.5-M) and Z-Image as base models, trained at a resolution of 512 2 512^{2} . With SD3.5-M, we study two non-differentiable rewards, OCR and GenEval, trained separately, and one multi-reward setting, PickScore + CLIPScore + HPSv2.1. For Z-Image, we use HPSv3 as reward. The generators are initialized as few-step distilled diffusion models. Prompt dataset. For OCR and GenEval, we use the corresponding training and test sets from Flow-GRPO. For all other rewards, we train on Pick-a-Pic ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) and evaluate on DrawBench ( Saharia et al., 2022 ) . Regardless of the training reward, we additionally evaluate every trained model on the OCR and GenEval test sets using their respective rewards. Reference pools. For OCR and GenEval, we generate reference pools with the base model using training-set prompts and 20 steps of sampling. For OCR, we generate eight candidates for each of 5,000 prompts and retain the highest-scoring candidate for each prompt only if its OCR reward is at least 0.6 0.6 . For GenEval, we construct a separate pool using 10,000 rows sampled from the GenEval training set. For all other rewards, we use the existing Pick-a-Pic images as the reference pool. Alternatively, an external model can generate the reference pool from the same training prompts: we use Nano Banana, Google’s proprietary image-generation model ( Google DeepMind, 2026 ) . Training and evaluation. Following prior work, we fine-tune the student generator using LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) with rank 32 32 and α = 64 \alpha=64 . Each epoch consists of 48 prompt groups, with group size K = 24 K{=}24 for the main results and K = 8 K{=}8 for all ablations. By default, the reward head is warmed up on samples from the reference distribution with scores from the reward, so that the generator does not receive noisy gradients early in training. This warm-up uses 1000 steps, a very small training budget compared with a full run ( Section 4.3 ). Both training and evaluation use four sampling steps, unless stated otherwise, with the LCM sampler ( Luo et al., 2023 ) and no classifier-free guidance (CFG scale 1 1 ). We also evaluate the trained models using Aesthetic and ImageReward on the same evaluation set. Details in Appendix B . 4.2 Task performance Text rendering. For the same training prompts, we compare a base-model pool , sampled from the base model, with a Nano Banana pool generated through its API. The two differ well beyond their scores: base-model samples keep SD3.5-M’s flat lighting, sparse layouts and misspelled words, whereas Nano Banana images are photographic, correctly lettered and set in fuller scenes. On OCR, the generator adopts the pool’s style without losing the text (last two rows of Fig. 3 ; more samples in Fig. 7 ): OCR stays at 0.92 0.92 ( Table 1 ), the aesthetic score rises from 5.46 5.46 to 5.62 5.62 , ImageReward, PickScore and HPS barely change, and CLIPScore drops from 28.75 28.75 to 26.86 26.86 . The two heads thus largely divide the work: the reward head governs what the reward measures, and the reference head governs everything the reward leaves unspecified, which is set by the reference pool. 5 Conclusion We presented DualHeads, a simple method for adapting few-step diffusion generators using only external reward evaluations and reference samples. It turns KL-regularized reward maximization into two binary classification problems, solved by lightweight heads on a frozen diffusion backbone.
